title: Spec-Driven Development with OpenSpec and GitHub Copilot
text:
Preface
AI-assisted development with tools like GitHub Copilot can be easy to start and difficult to control. A prompt can produce a plausible implementation in minutes, but plausibility is not the same as correctness. The hard questions remain: What are we building? Which parts of the existing system matter? How will we know that the result matches the intent?
This book is for software engineers, technical leads, and architects who want better answers to those questions without turning every change into a heavyweight ceremony. It introduces Spec-Driven Development (SDD) with OpenSpec as a practical way to make intent explicit, keep requirements close to implementation, and give GitHub Copilot the project context it needs. The examples move from greenfield work to brownfield systems, then through the less glamorous parts of real delivery: drift, verification, archiving, governance, and troubleshooting.
The approach has costs. Writing a useful spec takes time, and a vague or oversized spec can slow a team down instead of helping it. OpenSpec does not remove judgment from engineering, and Copilot can still misunderstand both the code and the specification. The goal is not to add paperwork for its own sake. It is to create a small, inspectable record of intent that helps people and tools make fewer expensive assumptions.
This book presents Spec-Driven Development (SDD) as a practical response to that continuity problem. It uses OpenSpec to keep requirements, proposed changes, design decisions, and implementation tasks in the repository where developers and agents can review them together.
The running example is a commercial truck search application. Its requirements change over three 90-minute mornings: the team first searches by a 15-character unit number, then adds VIN search, then shortens the unit-number limit and revises an active filter proposal. The changes are small enough to follow, but they expose the coordination problems that appear in larger systems.
This is not an argument for writing a specification before every code edit. Small, local, reversible changes may not justify the overhead. The workflow earns its cost when behavior crosses layers, requirements are likely to change, or several people and agent sessions need the same account of what the system should do.
Each part mirrors one morning of the training class. You can read the book independently or use its exercises as the class lab guide.

1.2 How SDD and OpenSpec help

What would change if agreed behavior moved out of a single Copilot session and into reviewable repository artifacts?
OpenSpec offers a place for that behavior beside the code, along with a workflow for proposing, applying, and archiving changes. What does that make easier to review later?

title: 1  From Chat Sessions to Durable Intent
text:
1.3 The coordination problem

Start with a developer who asks Copilot to implement a change and ends the session with plausible code. What does the next person inherit?
Follow the next developer or agent session, which can see the code but not the discarded alternatives and final decisions from the original conversation.
The implementation may satisfy a reasonable interpretation while still violating the business intent. How would the team recognize that gap?
Three things are easy to confuse: what the agent can generate, what the team has agreed to build, and what the tests prove. How might separating them change the conversation?

1.4 Jira, chat, and repository artifacts

What jobs belong to a Jira story, a chat transcript, code, tests, and a specification?
Jira can track the request, ownership, priority, and delivery status. OpenSpec can record behavior, proposed change, design decisions, and implementation tasks. Where should each piece of information live?
Why would neither a Jira story nor a chat transcript replace the other artifacts?

section: 1.5 When a specification earns its cost
text:
1.5 When a specification earns its cost

Before choosing the workflow, consider four conditions: change risk, ambiguity, coordination cost, and reversibility.
A full specification may make sense when behavior crosses the backend and frontend, requirements may change, or multiple developers and agent sessions need the same intent.
A smaller record or direct edit may be enough for a change that is local, obvious, and easy to reverse.
There is a real cost: a specification can become ceremony or stale documentation when the team does not review and update it. What review habit would keep that from happening?

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.1 Learning objective
Write observable requirements and scenarios that constrain implementation without prescribing its REST endpoints, database queries, or Angular components.
crumbs: Part I: Why Durable Intent Matters

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.2 How SDD supports the objective
An agent can turn an underspecified Jira story into a plausible implementation quickly. That speed can make an unanswered question expensive: the agent might choose a validation rule, a matching strategy, or an error response before anyone notices the decision.
One way to handle that risk is to move those decisions into a reviewable specification before implementation begins. The requirements can describe behavior, the scenarios can make that behavior observable, and the design can record the technical choices needed to implement it. OpenSpec keeps those concerns in separate artifacts, which gives the agent something more stable than a chat transcript to work from.
The specification does not replace judgment. When the team has not decided what should happen, it can be better to preserve that question for review than to hide an agent’s guess in code.
crumbs: Part I: Why Durable Intent Matters
3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.3 From acceptance criteria to requirements
The running example starts with a Jira request for exact search by a 15-character truck unit number. That sentence identifies the capability, but it does not describe every behavior that implementation and verification need. Before creating the change, ask which inputs are valid, what happens when the input is missing or invalid, what a match returns, and what the user sees when no record matches.
Once a decision is settled, turn it into a normative requirement. SHALL or MUST can mark behavior that is required, while definitions can narrow terms that might otherwise invite different interpretations. For example, the specification needs a shared meaning for 15 characters, exact match, missing, and invalid.
Keep the requirement at the business-behavior level. It might state that a valid unit number returns matching vehicles without requiring a particular controller method, SQL predicate, repository class, or Angular component. Those choices can live in design.md and in the implementation tasks.

3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.4 Scenario design
Given/When/Then scenarios offer one way to turn a requirement into an observable check:

Given establishes the relevant state and input.
When names the user or system action.
Then states the result that a reviewer, test, or running system can observe.

For the unit-number search, scenarios might cover valid input, invalid input, a matching record, and no matching record. A boundary scenario is most useful when the boundary represents required behavior, such as the difference between a 15-character value and a value that exceeds the allowed length.
It is useful to keep the scenarios independent of implementation. A scenario can require that an invalid value is rejected without prescribing whether validation occurs in a controller, service, or Angular form. That separation gives the team room to change the technical design without silently changing the agreed behavior.
crumbs: Part I: Why Durable Intent Matters
3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
section: 3.5 Tests can prove the wrong thing
text:
3.5 Tests can prove the wrong thing
Green tests provide evidence that an assertion passed. They do not, by themselves, show that the assertion came from an accepted requirement. An agent might write a test around an unsupported assumption, make the implementation satisfy that test, and report success while the product behavior remains wrong.
Before applying the change, trace each scenario to an observable result. During implementation, record which code and test provide that evidence. If a test has no corresponding scenario, ask whether it protects a real requirement or merely reflects an implementation detail. If a scenario has no evidence, the change may not be ready to verify.

text:
3.6 Hands-on exercise
Rewrite the 15-character unit-number story as OpenSpec requirements and Given/When/Then scenarios. Separate the behavior from the technical design. Record unresolved questions rather than choosing answers silently, then review the result with a partner before implementation.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.7 Verification checkpoint
For each requirement, it helps to check four things:

The language has one interpretation.
The behavior can be observed without reading the implementation.
The requirement stays within the change’s scope.
At least one meaningful scenario provides evidence for it.

Then inspect the scenarios as a set. Together, they can cover the settled valid, invalid, match, and no-match behavior without adding technical choices that the requirements do not need.

3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.8 What you learned
A requirement describes behavior the system must provide. A scenario makes one behavior concrete and testable. A design choice explains how the team plans to implement it. A test provides evidence that an implemented behavior produced an expected result. Keeping those roles distinct can give the agent a bounded target and give the team a way to review whether the target was met.

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.1 Learning objective
The exercises in Part II use two prepared repositories: commercial-truck-search-api and commercial-truck-search-ui. The backend owns the OpenAPI contract, and OpenAPI Generator produces the TypeScript Angular client consumed by the frontend. Before asking an agent to change behavior, you may want to establish a baseline for both repositories. That gives you a way to distinguish an environment problem from a specification or implementation defect.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to clone, inspect, build, test, and run both repositories. You will also have a record of the tool versions, application ports, and clean commits that can help you repeat the later exercises.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
section: 5.2 How the lab supports the objective
text:
5.2 How the lab supports the objective

You can use the prepared repositories to keep the exercises focused on SDD rather than project scaffolding.
You can keep an independent OpenSpec history beside each codebase.
The backend can remain the API owner while the frontend client is generated from that contract.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.3 Backend baseline
It may help to inspect the backend before changing it. Check the versions and tools in use: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1, Maven, Spring Data JPA, and H2. Locate the existing test conventions and application boundaries. Also check whether truck search has been implemented. Later chapters use its absence as the starting condition for the first feature.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.4 Frontend baseline
Inspect the frontend separately. Check for Angular 21 and Node.js 24.19.0, then locate the Vitest, component-test, Playwright, and generated-client boundaries. Record the local backend and frontend ports from the prepared repositories. The two applications may not use the same defaults in every environment.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
section: 5.5 VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA setup
text:
5.5 VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA setup
Open both repositories in VS Code or IntelliJ IDEA. Check that GitHub Copilot Chat is available in the IDE you plan to use, then record which terminal, task runner, and project view you used for each command. The commands and files remain the same, although each IDE exposes them differently. Keeping that difference visible can help separate an IDE problem from a repository problem.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.6 Hands-on exercise

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.8 What you learned
A known baseline gives later failures a reference point. If a starter repository does not build or its existing tests do not pass, fix or record that environment problem before an agent implements a feature. That leaves the next chapter free to focus on configuring OpenSpec rather than debugging an unexamined starting state.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.2 What initialization adds
When you initialize a repository, OpenSpec generates GitHub Copilot integration files from a selected profile. These files can keep repository-specific constraints close to the code they govern and make the configuration visible in version control. That makes them a reasonable place to start, although the generated profile may still need repository-specific review.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.3 Install and inspect the CLI
You can install the pinned OpenSpec package with npm. It is worth checking that the CLI reports version 1.13.1 and inspecting the available commands before initializing either repository.
It helps to keep two maintenance actions separate:

Upgrade the package when the team changes the OpenSpec CLI version.
Run openspec update when the team needs to refresh repository integrations from the installed package.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.4 Configure the backend repository
In the backend repository, you can initialize GitHub Copilot support with the profile that covers Java, Spring Boot, Maven, JPA, H2, testing, and OpenAPI ownership. Before committing the generated files, review them to see whether the repository-specific rules describe the backend rather than the frontend.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.5 Configure the frontend repository
In the frontend repository, you can initialize GitHub Copilot support with the profile that covers Angular, the generated client, Vitest, component tests, and Playwright. Backend implementation rules generally belong in the backend repository. The frontend consumes the backend contract, but it does not own the backend implementation.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec

6.7 Verification checkpoint: inspect the result
For a newly initialized repository, consider running the version, status, validation, and health checks that apply. These checks should let you confirm that:

the CLI reports OpenSpec 1.13.1;
each repository has the expected generated integration files;
validation accepts the generated configuration; and
the health check reports a usable initialization.

Reviewing the generated diff before committing can show what initialization added. The repository instructions can then remain the team-owned description of local constraints.

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.1 Learning objective
Exploration can help resolve business uncertainty before implementation artifacts are created. By the end of this chapter, you should have a decision record that describes what the unit-number search may need to do, which questions remain open, and who owns the next answer.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.2 How exploration supports the objective
Exploration works best as a thinking step rather than an implementation request. The agent can inspect the repositories, compare existing conventions, and expose questions that a short Jira story leaves unstated. A plausible guess should not become a requirement just because it makes the next prompt easier to write.
This distinction can matter for a full-stack change. The backend and frontend will usually need to agree on the meaning of a unit number, the shape of a successful result, and the way failures appear to the user. An unresolved decision in one repository may become a contract mismatch in the other.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.3 Start from the Jira story
A useful starting point is the request to search by a 15-character unit number. Read the story as a source of stated intent rather than as a complete specification. Extract the acceptance criteria exactly as they are written, then mark any behavior that the story implies but does not define.
It can help to keep the Jira issue connected to the future OpenSpec work. The issue provides the business context; the proposal and specifications can describe the behavior that the team agrees to build. Preserving that link gives reviewers a way to move from the requested change to the artifacts that explain its scope.
During exploration, ask the agent to inspect the relevant backend and frontend conventions. The goal is not to produce proposal.md, design.md, or tasks.md yet. The goal is to discover which decisions those artifacts will have to record.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.4 Questions that shape the behavior
The phrase “search by a 15-character unit number” may leave several implementation-blocking questions open:

Does the search require an exact match, or may it return partial matches?
Does the system normalize input before searching? If so, which characters or formats does it accept?
What should happen when the input is empty or malformed?
What should happen when the input is valid but no unit matches it?
What fields belong in the result, and how should the frontend display them?
Which errors belong in the API response, and which should become user-visible messages?
Which related capabilities are explicitly out of scope for this change?

These questions are better answered with the repository’s existing behavior, the business owner’s decision, or an explicit deferral than with a guess based on the ticket’s wording. A decision record can keep the uncertainty visible:








Question
Decision or status
Owner or next action




Exact or partial matching?
Open
Confirm with the business owner


Empty and malformed input?
Open
Compare existing validation conventions


Unknown unit number?
Open
Define the API and UI behavior together


Result shape?
Open
Agree on the backend-owned contract


Non-goals?
Open
Record deferred search capabilities



The table can be useful even before it contains many answers. It keeps an unanswered question visible instead of allowing it to disappear into generated code, and it gives the eventual proposal a clearer boundary.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.5 Compare exploration in both IDEs
Running the exploration workflow in VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA can provide a useful comparison. The model may use different wording, organize its findings differently, or notice different repository details in each environment. That variation is not necessarily a problem. The decisions that affect the change still need one agreed record.
Compare the results for coverage rather than prose. Did both explorations identify the same implementation-blocking questions? Did either one infer behavior that the Jira story does not state? Did either one miss a repository convention that the other found? Resolve those differences with evidence or mark them for an owner. A response that sounds more confident is not by itself a reason to choose its answer.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.6 Hands-on exercise
You can run the OpenSpec exploration workflow against the unit-number search request. Start with the Jira story, inspect the relevant repository conventions, and record the decisions and open questions. Repeating the exploration in VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA may expose differences worth resolving before the findings are combined into one agreed decision record.
Change artifacts can wait during this exercise. The intended output is the decision record, not an early proposal built on assumptions. Once the behavior is understood well enough to review, the next chapter can turn that record into coordinated backend and frontend proposal artifacts.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.7 Verification checkpoint
Before leaving exploration, it is worth checking every question that could block implementation. Each one should have an answer, an owner, or an explicit deferral. Also confirm that the record distinguishes:

behavior stated by the Jira story;
behavior inferred from existing repository conventions; and
behavior that still requires a business or technical decision.

If those categories are mixed together, more exploration may be needed. If they are clear, the team may have enough information to decide whether to propose the change or continue investigating.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.8 What you learned
Exploration can reduce risk when the request names a capability but leaves its observable behavior open. It gives the team a place to resolve cross-repository decisions before those decisions are copied into API code, frontend state, and tests.
A well-understood change may move directly to proposal. An unclear change may need more exploration rather than a more elaborate implementation prompt. The next artifact should record agreed behavior and remaining boundaries instead of hiding uncertainty behind confident language.

text:
8.1 Learning objective
The exploration record from the previous chapter gives the unit-number search its intended meaning. This chapter uses those decisions to shape artifacts that another developer could review and apply. The backend and frontend remain separate changes, while sharing one behavioral contract.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to create and review proposal, specification, design, and task artifacts for the first truck-search capability. You should also be able to tell whether the two repository changes are ready to apply or still depend on an unresolved decision.

title: 8  Proposing the First Full-Stack Change
text:
8.2 How proposal supports the objective
A proposal can explain why the change exists and where it stops. A specification can state what a user or client can observe. A design can explain how the repository might implement that behavior. Tasks can then make the work executable in dependency order.
OpenSpec keeps these answers in separate artifacts because they serve different readers and can change at different rates. The proposal gives reviewers a view of scope. The delta specification gives the team testable behavior. The design records implementation choices. The task list gives the agent and developer a sequence to follow.
An unresolved question from the exploration record would not belong in a requirement. It could be resolved with its owner or kept visible as a proposal dependency. A confident sentence in the wrong artifact would still describe an unresolved decision.

8.3 Start with two linked changes
One workable approach is to create an active change in each repository. The backend change would own the API contract, while the frontend change would consume it through the generated TypeScript client. Each repository would therefore have its own proposal, delta specification, design, and tasks, while the two changes shared terms and ordering constraints.

The decision record from chapter 7 can supply the entries in this table. The table is not meant to create new behavior. Its purpose is to expose ownership before the two proposals begin to drift.

text:
8.6 Order the tasks
Tasks work best when a developer can tell what must happen first and what evidence closes each task. A typical dependency order might be:

Record the backend proposal and delta specification from the agreed decisions.
Record the backend design, including the contract and test boundaries.
Implement and test the backend behavior, then publish the OpenAPI document.
Import the reviewed contract into the frontend repository and generate the client.
Record and implement the frontend states and interaction.
Run the frontend tests and the cross-application verification path.

The active OpenSpec tasks can describe this order without claiming that code exists before the apply step. A task would be complete once its code, artifact, or verification evidence exists. If a frontend task depends on an OpenAPI detail that the backend proposal has not settled, that question would need to return to review before implementation continues.

text:
8.7 Review the artifacts
It can help to review the two changes as one capability. Start with the exploration record, then follow each requirement into its design decision and tasks. A traceability table can make that review easier:

Rows for the remaining scenarios from the decision record can be added. A blank design or task cell would suggest that the proposal is incomplete. A task with no requirement or necessary design decision might be a candidate for removal.
During review, look for three common defects:

duplicated rules whose wording differs between repositories;
assumptions presented as accepted behavior;
implementation details placed in requirements without a reason.

It is also worth checking names and meanings across the contract. A result called “empty” in the backend would normally remain an empty state in the frontend unless the agreed behavior says otherwise.

title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
text:
9.1 Learning objective
The reviewed backend proposal, specification, design, and task sequence can now guide the code change. The aim is to preserve the behavior those artifacts describe while keeping implementation choices inside the approved design boundary.
By the end of this chapter, you can apply the unit-number change in the Spring Boot repository and trace each backend scenario to implementation code, a meaningful assertion, and local verification output.

title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
text:
9.2 How apply supports the objective
The task list provides the starting point for implementation. You can follow its accepted order instead of reconstructing intent from an earlier chat session or the original request. When a task exposes a missing requirement or an implementation choice outside the reviewed design, stop and return that question to review. An unresolved decision needs an answer before it becomes code.
Update task state only when the related code and evidence agree. A changed file is not evidence that the behavior works, and a passing test is not enough if the test asserts the wrong behavior.

9.4 Contract ownership
Treat the backend as the owner of the API contract. Generate the OpenAPI document from the implemented API, then inspect it before handing it to the Angular repository. Check the request constraints, response types, and error responses against the reviewed specification.
The generated document is part of the evidence for the backend change. If it omits a constraint, uses the wrong response shape, or describes an error as a success response, the mismatch points to an implementation defect. The frontend repository should not have to compensate by maintaining a second version of the contract.

title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
text:
9.5 Backend tests
Add focused unit tests where isolation clarifies validation, service, or error behavior. Add Spring Boot integration tests for the scenarios that require the application, persistence, or HTTP boundary together.
For each specified scenario, check that the test exercises the relevant boundary and asserts an observable result. Review the assertions for accidental agreement with the implementation. A test that copies an incorrect status code or response shape from the implementation may stay green while the contract is wrong.

10.1 Learning objective
The backend change is now implemented and its OpenAPI document can serve as the handoff artifact. 10.2 How the contract supports the objective
In this workflow, the backend owns the API contract while the frontend handles the interaction with that contract and the way its results appear to a user. Keeping those responsibilities separate gives the two repositories a useful boundary:

title: 10  Applying the Angular Change
text:
10.3 Generate the client
Start from the OpenAPI document produced and inspected in the previous chapter. Recording the revision or commit that supplied it makes the client reproducible for another developer.
Before generation, inspect the frontend repository instructions and its existing generated-client configuration. Check the output directory, naming conventions, package version, and the command the repository uses for generation. The exact command belongs to the prepared repository, so a one-off command from a different project could produce misleading output.
Run the configured OpenAPI Generator task, then inspect the diff. The generated output is expected to contain the request and response types, service methods, and transport configuration described by the document. Before writing component code, check whether:

the unit-number constraint appears where the generator exposes it;
the success response has the fields the frontend scenario needs;
the no-match and error responses remain distinguishable; and
the generated service points at the expected local backend URL for the test environment.

Keeping generated files in their configured directory and leaving them unedited gives application decisions a clear home in hand-written services, components, and tests. Regenerate when the backend contract changes, when the generator configuration changes, or when a clean checkout cannot reproduce the same client. A generated diff can provide evidence of a contract change to review rather than noise to hide.

title: 10  Applying the Angular Change
text:
10.4 Implement the search experience
Read the frontend delta specification before choosing Angular boundaries. The UI needs to make the specified behavior visible without duplicating the backend’s implementation.

10.4.1 Input and validation
Bind the search control to the input described by the specification. Client-side validation can cover rules the frontend is allowed to know, such as the settled length or empty input behavior. The backend still provides the final check because a client-side validation rule can be bypassed or become stale after the contract changes.
Keep validation messages tied to the actual state of the control. The UI can avoid sending a request for input the specification says is invalid, and it should distinguish a valid search with no record from a backend error.


10.4.2 Request and display states
Model the states the user can observe. At minimum, the component or its view model will usually need a clear path for:

the initial state before a search;
loading while the request is in progress;
a matching result;
a valid search with no matching record; and
an API or network error.

Each state benefits from one visible outcome and an appropriate transition. When a second search starts, the result from the first request should not appear to belong to the second. If the frontend specification allows retrying, a failure can give the user a way to recover without a page reload.
Route the request through the generated client, preferably behind a small hand-written service or facade when that matches the repository’s existing Angular design. The component can then coordinate input and presentation without knowing URL paths, serializing request bodies, or reproducing the generated response type.

title: 10  Applying the Angular Change
text:
10.6 Frontend tests
Use the narrowest test that provides meaningful evidence for the behavior under review.

Use Vitest for pure validation or state-transition logic when the repository keeps that logic separate from Angular rendering.
Use Angular component tests for control interaction, generated-client calls, loading behavior, result rendering, empty states, and error states. Stub the generated client at the service boundary instead of testing generated code.
Use Playwright for the browser-to-backend path. Start the applications on the recorded lab ports or the repository’s configured test ports, then assert the user-visible result rather than an internal component field.

Review the test doubles alongside the production code. A mock that always returns a result cannot prove the empty state, and a test that asserts a method was called says little about what the user saw. For each scenario, assert the observable state and, where relevant, that invalid input did not produce an API call.

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.1 Learning objective
The backend and frontend changes now exist in two repositories. A passing test in either repository may not, by itself, show that the change is complete. This chapter separates the evidence gathered by validation, implementation review, synchronization, and archival.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to validate the OpenSpec artifacts, compare the implementation with the accepted change, synchronize accepted deltas into the main specifications, and archive a completed change without losing its history.
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.2 Four different checks
These checks address different questions. Running one generally does not replace the others.








Check
Question it answers
Evidence it produces




Artifact validation
Are the proposal, requirements, design, and tasks structured correctly?
The OpenSpec CLI result and any reported structural errors


Implementation verification
Does the code and its test suite implement the accepted behavior?
Code review, focused tests, integration evidence, and the task status


Synchronization
Have accepted requirements moved into the main specifications?
Updated main specs and the retained change record


Archival
Is the change complete and recoverable after active work closes?
An archived change containing its reason, decisions, and evidence



Artifact validation is usually the cheapest check, so you might run it first. It can catch a malformed artifact or a missing required section. It cannot prove that the application behaves correctly, that the tests exercise the right path, or that the two repositories agree.
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.3 Validate the artifacts
Run the OpenSpec validation command configured for the repository. You will usually want to validate the backend and frontend change directories separately because each repository owns its own code, tests, and specification context.
Read the result rather than treating a successful exit code as the whole review. Check that the validator examined the expected change and that the reported paths match the artifacts you edited. If validation fails, repair the artifact structure before asking Copilot to inspect the implementation. A code review built on an incomplete change description may otherwise have no stable target.
Validation also has a useful limit: it checks the shape and rules the CLI knows about. It does not decide whether a requirement is complete, whether a design is coherent, or whether an accepted scenario works in a running application.
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.4 Verify the implementation
Compare the implementation with the proposal, requirements, design, and tasks. It helps to start with the requirements and scenarios because they describe the behavior a user or another system can observe. You can then use the design and tasks to check whether the implementation follows the agreed boundaries.
For the unit-number change, one useful inspection order follows the contract:

Verify the backend behavior and its API document.
Check that the frontend client was generated from that reviewed API document.
Check the frontend states against the frontend requirements.
Run the cross-repository path and confirm the browser-visible result.

This order can make a contract mismatch easier to locate. If the backend behavior or API document is wrong, the backend-owned artifact is the natural place to repair it. If the contract is correct but the UI is missing a scenario, the frontend implementation or its tests may need the repair. Adding an undocumented workaround to one repository can make the other appear complete without resolving the underlying gap.
Use the task list as a checklist, not as proof. A completed task means that someone marked it complete. The tests and review still need to show that the accepted behavior works and that the implementation remains coherent with the design.
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.5 Synchronize accepted changes
Synchronization moves an accepted delta into the main specifications. In OpenSpec 1.13.1, it is useful to treat sync as a specification update, not as a code-generation or test command. Before running it, check that the implementation is complete, the tests pass, and the change has been accepted by the team.
Inspect the main specifications before synchronization. Note which requirements already exist, which are new, and which accepted behavior the delta changes. Then run the repository’s configured sync workflow and inspect the resulting diff. Look for the accepted behavior in the main specifications, while checking that conditions remain present and the change record remains intact.
Repeat the inspection after synchronization. Check that:

the main specifications describe the behavior now implemented;
unchanged requirements remain unchanged;
the delta still records why the change was made; and
identifiers such as the Jira issue and cross-repository change identifier remain attached.

If the diff changes more than the accepted delta, pause and review the generated or proposed update. Treat synchronization as a specification update, rather than a way to resolve ambiguity by editing the specification until it fits the code.

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.7 The fresh-session test
A useful check after archival is to start a new Copilot session. Provide the repository artifacts, not the previous chat transcript, and ask what the unit-number change requires. See whether the session can recover the accepted behavior from the main specifications and the archived change.
This test can expose decisions that still exist only in someone’s memory. When the fresh session cannot recover a condition, identifier, or boundary, return to the specifications or archive and record it there. A remembered conversation does not belong to the repository’s source of truth.
crumbs: Part III: Applying and Evolving the Specification

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.8 Hands-on exercise
Validate, verify, synchronize when appropriate, and archive the unit-number changes in both repositories.

Run artifact validation in each repository and repair any structural failure.
Compare the backend and frontend implementation with their accepted requirements, designs, and tasks.
Run the focused tests and the cross-repository verification path.
Inspect the main specifications, synchronize the accepted deltas, and review the resulting diff.
Preserve the Jira and cross-repository identifiers, then archive only after both repositories meet the completion conditions.
Start a fresh Copilot session and recover the accepted behavior from repository artifacts.

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.9 Verification checkpoint
The unit-number change may be ready to close when the main specifications are coherent, active tasks are complete, the tests and cross-repository path pass, and the archived artifacts preserve the reason for the change. If any of those conditions is missing, consider leaving the change active and recording the missing evidence.

11.10 What you learned
Validation checks artifact structure. Tests and review verify behavior. Synchronization records accepted behavior in the main specifications. Archiving closes the active change while preserving the decisions and identifiers needed to recover it later.

A change is generally ready to close when every ADDED requirement works and accepted unit-number behavior remains unchanged. The evidence should cover the full 17-character VIN rule, mode selection, mode-specific validation, the backend contract, and the frontend path. It should also include the regression tests for unit-number consumers.
If a test or review finds a contradiction, the change should stay open. Update the delta or the implementation at the boundary where the behavior is wrong, then repeat the focused verification. The new VIN path working by itself would not be enough reason to archive the change.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.1 Learning objective
By the end of this chapter, you can replace an accepted requirement without leaving contradictory rules in the source of truth. You can also trace the replacement through the backend contract, the generated Angular client, the UI, and the tests in both repositories.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.2 Start with the accepted requirement
The original unit-number rule allows a value with 15 characters. Because that rule is already accepted, the new request would change behavior that the repositories already describe and implement rather than add a separate feature.
You can begin by locating the accepted requirement and its scenarios. It helps to record the exact rule being replaced, then list the behavior that should remain unchanged. That list is useful because changing a length constraint can affect more than one boundary. Normalization, empty input, invalid input, matching, and the result shown for a match or no match may each have their own scenario.
The change proposal should answer these questions before implementation:

Which accepted requirement is being replaced?
What does the revised maximum mean at the boundary of 10 characters?
Does normalization happen before the length check, and does the change alter that behavior?
What happens for empty input?
Which existing match, no-match, and error behavior remains unchanged?

If the team has not decided one of these points, it may be better to keep it open for review. An agent should not choose a rule merely because the code currently makes that choice.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.3 Write a complete modification
OpenSpec distinguishes a modified requirement from an added requirement. An added requirement introduces behavior that did not exist in the accepted specification. A modified requirement replaces the accepted requirement with a new complete version.
For this change, the delta would replace the 15-character rule with a maximum of 10 characters. It should carry revised scenarios for the valid boundary, values beyond the boundary, empty input, normalization, and the behavior that remains unchanged. The exact scenarios depend on the decisions made during exploration, but the delta needs to contain those decisions rather than pointing back to an old rule and asking the implementer to combine the two.
Appending a second requirement that says “maximum 10 characters” would leave both rules in the source of truth. A reader could not tell whether 15 characters is still valid, whether the newer rule has priority, or which scenarios belong to which rule. The implementation agent would face the same ambiguity. Modification semantics remove the old rule and make the revised requirement the one that survives synchronization into the main specification.
Review the delta as a set of operations:

ADDED introduces a new requirement.
MODIFIED replaces an accepted requirement and carries its complete revised behavior.
REMOVED deletes a requirement that no longer applies.
RENAMED changes the requirement’s identity while preserving the intended behavior.

The distinction that matters here is between ADDED and MODIFIED. The unit-number length change fits MODIFIED because the new rule replaces an accepted one.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.4 Full-stack impact
The accepted requirement may appear in more places than the main specification. A search of both repositories for the old constraint can establish the impact surface before the change is applied. The search can include the OpenSpec artifacts, backend validation, OpenAPI constraints, generated client output, frontend validation, UI text, and tests. It does not by itself decide which files should change.
Backend validation can enforce the revised rule, while the OpenAPI contract describes the same constraint. Inspecting the generated contract before regenerating the Angular client gives the team a chance to catch a mismatch. The frontend can then consume the reviewed contract rather than preserve an older generated constraint.
Frontend validation and any UI text that still describes 15 characters would also need an update. The existing search behavior that the delta explicitly preserves can remain unchanged. A passing test for a ten-character value would not be enough if a test, error message, or generated schema still accepts or describes the old limit.
Use the tests to cover both sides of the replacement:

the new maximum and the value beyond it;
normalization and empty input, according to the reviewed decisions;
preserved match, no-match, and error behavior; and
consistent validation across the backend and Angular client.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.5 Hands-on exercise
The exercise is to implement and archive the revised unit-number rule in both repositories. The change record can keep the sequence visible:

Locate the accepted 15-character requirement and its scenarios.
Decide the revised boundary, normalization, empty-input, and preserved-behavior rules.
Create a MODIFIED delta containing the complete replacement requirement and scenarios.
Update backend validation and the OpenAPI constraint.
Regenerate the Angular client and update frontend validation, UI text, and affected tests.
Verify the implementation against the delta before synchronizing and archiving it.

At each step, compare the latest artifact with the previous accepted behavior. If implementation work reveals an unanswered product decision, pause and revise the delta. Resolving the gap with a code-only change or a corrective chat message would leave the source of truth unchanged.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.7 What you learned
A modified delta works as a replacement rather than an additional opinion about the same behavior. Carrying the complete revised requirement and its scenarios helps prevent the old and new unit-number rules from coexisting accidentally. Searching the repositories and generated outputs then checks whether the replacement reached every boundary where the accepted rule was used.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.1 Learning objective
By the end of this chapter, you can revise an active change when the business changes its mind before implementation is complete. You can also decide whether the revision belongs in the existing change or in a separate one, then trace the decision through the specifications, API, UI, generated client, and tests.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
section: 14.2 Start with the decision that changed
text:
14.2 Start with the decision that changed
An active change can be treated as a working agreement rather than a permanent commitment. The team may discover a missing business rule, reject an earlier assumption, or widen the requested behavior during implementation. When that happens, the next step is usually to update the artifact that records the decision. A corrective message in chat may reach the current implementer, but it does not update the instructions that reviewers, later agents, or the next developer will read.
The interrupted proposal in this chapter began with one filter:

filter vehicles by Fleet Origin State;
add Active Status values of Active and Decommissioned; and
decide how the filters combine and how empty selections behave.

The new request changes the shape of that work. It is no longer enough to implement the original filter and append a second control. The proposal needs to describe the combined behavior that the user now expects.
Before changing the artifact, write down the decision that moved. Ask:

Is Active Status an additional filter, or does it replace part of the original proposal?
Do the filters combine with AND, OR, or a rule that depends on the selected values?
What does an empty Fleet Origin State selection mean?
What does an empty Active Status selection mean?
Which completed work still supports the revised behavior?

It helps to keep unanswered questions visible during review. Reviewers should not have to infer product behavior from whatever the current query or UI happens to do.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.3 Rebuild the active artifact
Once the decision is clear, revise the active change as a complete description of the new behavior. Revisit its scope, affected capabilities, requirements, scenarios, and task list. Stale text is usually better replaced than left beside a second statement for the reader to reconcile.
The revision will usually need to make these relationships explicit:

the filter controls available to the user;
the values each control accepts;
how multiple selections combine;
what the API receives when a control has no selection; and
what results and empty states the UI presents.

Then trace the effects through the implementation. A change to filter behavior can affect API parameters, query construction, validation, generated-client types, UI controls, and tests. The exact files depend on the two repositories, but the artifact should name the affected surfaces before implementation resumes.
It is also worth revisiting tasks in the same pass. A completed task remains complete only when its result still satisfies the revised requirement. A task that implemented the one-filter query may need to be reopened if the new combination rule invalidates that query. A task that added shared plumbing may remain complete if the revised scenarios still exercise it.
This distinction helps avoid two common errors. Marking every earlier task incomplete throws away work that the new design still uses. Leaving every task complete hides work that no longer proves the requested behavior.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
section: 14.4 Decide whether to amend or split the change
text:
14.4 Decide whether to amend or split the change
Not every new request belongs in the active proposal. Four questions can help with the decision:

How much implementation is already complete?
Does the new request change the same behavior or introduce an independent capability?
Does the release still treat both requests as one outcome?
Would a reviewer understand the final proposal without reconstructing its history?

The active change is usually the better home when the new decision corrects or completes the behavior already under review. The filter combination rule belongs with the filter proposal because it defines what that proposal means.
A separate change may be appropriate when the new request has an independent purpose, review path, or release decision. A separately valuable change is usually better kept outside the active proposal, even when the code touches the same screen. Shared files create coordination work, but they do not make two business decisions one change.
The change record can make that choice visible. A short note explaining why the proposal was amended or split gives reviewers a way to check the scope without relying on chat history.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.5 Keep implementation and review synchronized
After revising the artifact, review it before asking an agent to continue. The review can check whether the requirements and scenarios describe the same combination rules, whether the API contract can represent those rules, and whether the UI tasks still describe the original one-filter design.
Then compare existing work with the revised scenarios. For each completed item, ask what evidence it provides. Code that still passes a narrow unit test may not satisfy the revised behavior if the test never combines the filters. A generated client may compile while still exposing an obsolete parameter shape. A label or help message may describe only the first filter even after the query supports both.
When the review finds a gap, leave the proposal open. Revise the requirement or scenario first, then update the affected task and implementation. This order keeps the source of truth ahead of the code and gives the next verification pass a precise target.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.6 Hands-on exercise
Revise, review, apply, and verify the active filter change using the documented OpenSpec 1.13.1 workflows in both IDEs.

Locate the active change and record the original one-filter behavior.
Add the Active Status decision and resolve the filter-combination and empty-selection questions.
Revise the requirements and scenarios so they describe the complete combined behavior.
Reassess the API parameters, query design, generated client, UI controls, and affected tests.
Reopen or reorder tasks that the new decision invalidated, while preserving work that still provides evidence.
Review and apply the revised change, then verify the implementation before closing it.

At each step, compare the active artifact with the code and tests. If an implementation detail exposes an unanswered product decision, return to the artifact and record the decision there. A code-only patch or a chat message that disappears from the change history would leave that gap unresolved.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.8 What you learned
An in-flight change works best when its source of truth is updated before the work that depends on it is re-evaluated. The right unit of review is the behavior, not the number of files already changed. Completed work can remain in place when it still proves the revised scenarios, while work whose evidence the new decision invalidates may need to be reopened.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.1 Learning objective
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to manage concurrent changes without treating isolated folders or branches as proof that the changes are compatible. You should have a way to compare active deltas with the same accepted baseline, expose semantic overlap, and choose an archive order that can preserve both business decisions.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.2 Isolation is not compatibility
Parallel work tends to create two separate coordination problems. Git can isolate edits to files, and OpenSpec can isolate proposed intent in separate change folders. Neither mechanism, by itself, shows that the changes can be accepted together.
Two changes can pass their own reviews and tests while making incompatible decisions about the same behavior. They may add different values to one search contract, define different meanings for a shared request parameter, or ask the frontend to expose two controls that the backend cannot represent together. The conflict is semantic even when the files do not conflict textually.
It helps to keep the mechanisms distinct:

An OpenSpec change folder isolates a proposal, its requirements, design, and tasks from other proposals.
A Git branch isolates a line of commits from another line of commits.
A worktree gives a branch its own working directory so developers or agents can work in parallel.

These mechanisms can reduce accidental edits. They do not, on their own, answer whether the proposals describe one coherent product behavior. Comparing each proposal with the accepted specification and with the other active changes can answer that question more directly.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.3 A pair of truck-search changes
Consider two active changes in the truck-search system:

one adds License Plate search; and
another modifies VIN-related behavior.

The changes have different business goals, so separate proposals make sense at first. Each proposal should describe its own input rules, result behavior, and non-goals. The separation lets reviewers discuss one decision without mixing it with the other.
The proposals would still benefit from a shared-surface review. Compare them against the latest accepted specifications and inspect whether both changes affect:

the backend search contract;
the generated Angular client;
the control that selects or submits a search mode;
shared validation and error behavior; and
regression tests for the search modes that already work.

The purpose of this comparison need not be to reject parallel work. It can instead surface decisions that may need to be made once. For example, if both proposals change the shared search request, the team may need to agree on a request shape and mode-selection rule before either change becomes the new baseline. A frontend proposal that invents a client shape independently of the backend proposal may already be behind the source of truth.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.5 Coordinate the contract boundary
The backend owns the OpenAPI contract in this book’s two-repository lab. That ownership suggests a practical order for the parallel changes: agree on the backend behavior, review the resulting contract, then regenerate the Angular client before completing frontend work.
This order does not mean that frontend work has to wait for every backend task. A frontend developer can prepare tests or UI structure against a reviewed proposal. The generated client would still need to come from the accepted backend contract. A hand-written client type may hide an unresolved contract decision rather than solve it.
Keep the following questions visible while the changes are active:

Can the contract represent License Plate and VIN searches without ambiguous combinations?
Which input rules belong to each mode, and where are they enforced?
Does the shared UI expose the modes consistently with the contract?
Which existing unit-number and VIN scenarios must remain unchanged?
Which generated files and frontend tests must be regenerated or revised after synchronization?

An answer that applies to both proposals belongs in the shared specification or in an explicit coordination decision. An answer that applies to only one capability belongs in that change’s requirements. Keeping those scopes separate helps prevent a local assumption from becoming an accidental rule for every search mode.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.6 Reconcile and archive
Archive order can matter because synchronization changes the accepted baseline. The first archived change becomes the comparison point for the next one. In many cases, choosing the order from dependency makes more sense than choosing it from which developer finished first.
When the other change depends on a shared contract or prerequisite behavior, it usually makes sense to archive the change that establishes it first. If the changes are independent at the contract level, either order may work, but the second change still needs a fresh comparison against the updated baseline.
After the first change is synchronized and archived:

Re-read the second change against the latest main specifications.
Replace stale assumptions in its requirements, design, and tasks.
Recheck its API and generated-client impact against the accepted contract.
Re-run the overlap review and record any decision that changed.
Apply, verify, synchronize, and archive only after the revised change is coherent.

Avoid silently rewriting the second change to fit the first. If the first change changed a shared decision, update the second artifact so the new behavior remains reviewable. If the goals are no longer compatible, keep the second change open and ask for a product decision rather than preserving two contradictory rules in the main specification.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.7 Hands-on exercise
Create two active changes for the prepared truck-search repositories: one for License Plate search and one for a VIN-related behavior change.

Write the business goal, affected behavior, non-goals, and scenarios for each change.
Inspect both changes against the same accepted specifications.
Mark every shared backend contract, generated-client, UI, and regression-test surface.
Identify one semantic overlap and record the decision that resolves it.
Choose an archive order based on the dependency between the two changes.
Synchronize the first change, then revise the second against the new baseline.
Apply and verify the second change without removing either business goal.

At each step, compare the artifact with the implementation and tests. If a conflict appears only after the first change is archived, that is a sign that the second change may have become stale. A code patch that leaves the active artifact describing the old contract will make the discrepancy harder to review.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.9 What you learned
Parallel changes are independent proposals, but they do not necessarily become independent realities. Git branches and worktrees protect concurrent edits, while OpenSpec records the decisions each change intends to make. The team still needs to compare those decisions against one accepted baseline, coordinate shared contracts, and re-review any change that becomes stale after synchronization.

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.1 Learning objective
Establish a proportionate, reviewable OpenSpec workflow that can survive beyond the book’s exercises.
The exercises used one person, two repositories, and a controlled sequence of changes. A team has to answer harder questions: who owns a decision, how much specification work a change deserves, and how a reviewer can recover the reasoning after the original Copilot session is gone. SDD becomes a team practice when the repository records those decisions without turning every edit into a formal project.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.2 Put decisions in the right place
text:
16.2 Put decisions in the right place
An agent can propose code, tests, and artifact text. It cannot decide whether a business behavior is acceptable, whether a contract change is compatible with existing clients, or whether a risk is worth the cost. A human owner must make those decisions and leave enough evidence for another person to review them.
Use the repository artifacts for engineering intent and Jira for work tracking:

Jira records the work item, status, priority, and responsible people.
proposal.md records the business goal, scope, and non-goals for a change.
Delta specifications record the behavior the team will add, modify, or remove.
design.md records implementation decisions and their constraints.
tasks.md records the work sequence and its verification points.
Commits, pull requests, and test output provide evidence that the accepted intent was implemented.

This division prevents two common failures. A Jira ticket should not be the only place where an agent can find a behavioral rule, and an OpenSpec change should not become a second work-tracking system.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.3 Make traceability recoverable
Traceability is useful when it lets a reviewer move from a decision to its evidence without asking the original author to reconstruct the conversation. Define a small naming and linking convention for both repositories. For example, a Jira issue can link to the OpenSpec change name, the pull request can mention the same issue, and the verification record can point to the relevant test command or result.
The exact convention matters less than using it consistently. At minimum, a reviewer should be able to answer these questions:

Which business decision does this change implement?
Which requirements and scenarios express that decision?
Which code, generated artifacts, and tests carry it out?
What evidence supports synchronization and archive readiness?

Keep the links close to the artifacts they explain. A change that affects the backend contract and the Angular client should identify both repositories and the point at which the client must be regenerated. That makes the contract boundary visible during review instead of leaving it implicit in task order.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.4 Assign review ownership
Review ownership follows the decision being reviewed. The same person may hold several roles on a small change, but the roles should still be explicit.

A product or business owner reviews behavior, scope, and non-goals when the change affects what the system promises.
A technical reviewer checks contracts, architecture, data handling, and integration boundaries.
An implementation reviewer checks that code and tests satisfy the reviewed requirements.
The person responsible for synchronization or archival checks that the accepted specifications and evidence are complete.

These reviews do not require four people or four meetings. They require the team to name the questions that must be answered before work moves forward. A behavior change needs business review. An OpenAPI or persistence change needs technical review. A routine, reversible edit may need only a short recorded decision and focused verification.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.5 Scale the artifacts to the risk
text:
16.5 Scale the artifacts to the risk
OpenSpec is a control for uncertainty and coordination. It is not a requirement that every line change receive the same amount of ceremony. Before creating a full change, classify the work by its uncertainty, reversibility, and blast radius.
Use a lighter record for a routine, low-risk, reversible change whose behavior is already covered by the accepted specifications. Use a full proposal, delta specification, design, task list, and verification record when the change crosses a repository boundary, changes a contract, modifies accepted behavior, or creates a meaningful regression risk. Urgency does not remove the need to record a decision. It may justify a smaller initial artifact and a follow-up review.
Record deliberate exceptions. A short note should state why the full workflow was unnecessary and what evidence still supports the change. This gives the next reviewer a reason for the missing artifacts instead of making the repository look incomplete by accident.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.6 Maintain the context that agents use
text:
16.6 Maintain the context that agents use
The workflow itself changes over time. OpenSpec versions, Copilot integration files, generated clients, commands, and test tooling can all make an old instruction inaccurate. Treat those files as maintained engineering assets.
Review the repository context when you upgrade OpenSpec or the Copilot integration. Remove duplicated instructions when two files begin to disagree. Check command examples against the versions used by the repositories. Revisit generated integration files after an update rather than assuming that a new version preserves the old layout or behavior.
The same rule applies to the book’s examples. A command that worked for the prepared repositories at one version can become misleading after a tool upgrade. Keep version-sensitive guidance tied to a tested version, and make the version visible when a reader needs it to reproduce the result.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.7 Capstone: defend the amount of specification
text:
16.7 Capstone: defend the amount of specification
Complete the capstone by proposing a new commercial truck search change across both repositories. The purpose is not to produce the largest possible set of artifacts. It is to defend the amount of specification work the change needs.

State the business goal, affected behavior, non-goals, and owner.
Classify the change by uncertainty, reversibility, urgency, and blast radius.
Choose the OpenSpec artifacts that follow from that classification.
Record the backend contract boundary and the frontend impact, including generated-client work.
Assign business and technical review where the change requires those decisions.
Link the Jira issue, OpenSpec change, commits, pull requests, and verification evidence.
Apply, verify, synchronize, and archive the change only after the accepted specifications and implementation agree.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.8 Verification checkpoint
Ask a reviewer in a fresh session to reconstruct the capstone’s intent and evidence using repository artifacts alone. The reviewer should be able to identify the business decision, the changed behavior, the responsible reviewers, the contract boundary, and the evidence for completion without opening the originating chat session.
If the reviewer cannot do that, find the missing decision or link before treating the change as a team practice success. The problem may be an underspecified requirement, an unrecorded exception, a stale instruction, or a verification step that produced no recoverable evidence.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.9 What you learned
SDD works as an engineering control when the team records intent, assigns human ownership, scales the artifacts to the risk, and preserves evidence through synchronization and archive. It also has a cost: someone must review the decisions, maintain the context, and keep the artifacts current. A proportionate workflow makes that cost visible instead of hiding it in repeated rework or fragile agent sessions.
crumbs: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 17  Summary
text:
OpenSpec gives an AI-assisted team a durable place to keep intent, but the files alone do not create alignment. The team must still ask precise questions, review generated artifacts, test the implementation, and reconcile overlapping decisions.
The truck-search sequence demonstrates the core patterns:

A greenfield change establishes the first accepted behavior through explore, propose, apply, and archive.
An additive delta introduces VIN search without replacing unit-number search.
A modified delta replaces the old unit-number constraint with a maximum of 10 characters.
An active proposal can be revised before implementation when the business changes direction.
Parallel changes require both artifact isolation and source-control isolation, followed by deliberate synchronization.

The practical test is whether a developer or agent can enter the repository in a later session and recover what the system should do, what is changing, and how completion will be verified. When the specs, code, and tests answer those questions consistently, context has become shared engineering material rather than chat history.

title: Appendix B — OpenSpec CLI Command Reference
text:
B.1 Typical workflow
This appendix offers a quick reference for the openspec CLI commands used throughout the book. OpenSpec slash commands are covered in Appendix B. The CLI command names and examples are current as of OpenSpec CLI 1.13.1. Since your installed version may differ, you may want to run openspec --help or openspec <command> --help to check the syntax available to you.
The CLI helps manage the files and relationships that make a change reviewable. Decisions about a change’s scope and the quality of its requirements remain with the people reviewing the work.
OpenSpec reports failures through the process exit status, which makes commands such as validate suitable for scripts and CI. The CLI help does not promise a numbered list of exit codes, so this reference does not invent one. In a pipeline, treat a nonzero status as a failed check and preserve the command output as the diagnostic.

title: Appendix B — OpenSpec CLI Command Reference
text:
You might run openspec init once in a project, then use openspec update when the generated instruction files need to catch up.
To begin a change, use openspec new change <name>, then inspect its artifact status with openspec status --change <name>.
You can use openspec list, openspec show, openspec context, and openspec instructions to inspect the repository and work out what an agent needs next.
Before treating the change as ready, consider running openspec validate <name>. In CI, openspec validate --all may be a better fit when the repository is the unit of validation.
After implementation and verification, you can run openspec archive <name>. Archiving updates the main specifications and moves the completed change out of the active work area.

text:
B.2 Core commands
The commands below cover the operations most projects use regularly. The --json options can help when another tool needs to consume a result, but reading the Markdown artifacts still matters during review.








Command
Purpose
Useful options

Initialize OpenSpec in a project and write the selected tool instruction files.
--tools all, --tools github-copilot, --language <language>, --profile <profile>, --force


openspec update [path]
Update OpenSpec instruction files after the CLI or tool configuration changes.
--force


openspec new change <name>
Create a new change directory using the selected workflow schema.
--description <text>, --goal <text>, --schema <name>, --store <id>, --json


openspec list
List active changes.
--changes, --specs, --sort recent|name, --json, --store <id>


openspec show [item-name]
Display a change or specification.
--type change|spec, --json, --diff, --deltas-only, --store <id>


openspec status --change <id>
Show which artifacts are complete for a change.
--all, --schema <name>, --json, --store <id>


openspec validate [item-name]
Validate a change or specification.
--all, --changes, --specs, --strict, --json, --type change|spec, --store <id>

--yes, --skip-specs, --no-validate, --json, --store <id>


openspec doctor
Report relationship health for the resolved OpenSpec root.
--json, --store <id>



The command names reflect two related interfaces. openspec new change creates a change. The older grouped forms, openspec change show, openspec change list, and openspec change validate, can inspect and validate changes. Since the help output marks openspec change list as deprecated, new scripts are better served by the top-level list, show, and validate commands.
For a quick inspection of a repository, you could start with:
openspec list
openspec status --all
openspec doctor
For a CI (continuous integration) check that covers both active and archived material, choose the narrowest validation that matches the pipeline’s purpose. openspec validate --all validates all changes and specifications, while openspec validate --archived checks that archived changes have completed tasks.

B.3 Store and workset commands
Stores and worksets address different needs. You can think of a store as a standalone OpenSpec repository registered on the local machine, giving several related projects a shared place for specifications and changes. A workset is a personal, local view that composes folders for a working session. Removing a workset does not remove its member folders.








Command
Purpose
Useful options




openspec store setup [id]
Create and register a local store.
--path <path>, --remote <url>, --init-git, --no-init-git, --json


openspec store register [path]
Register an existing local store.
--id <id>, --yes, --json


openspec store list
List stores registered on this machine.
--json


openspec store doctor [id]
Check a store’s registration and metadata.
--json


openspec store unregister <id>
Forget a registration without deleting the files.
--json


openspec store remove <id>
Forget a registration and delete its local folder.
--yes, --json


openspec context
Print the working context for the resolved OpenSpec root.
--json, --store <id>, --code-workspace <path>, --force


openspec workset create [name]
Save a named view of project folders.
Repeat --member <path>; optionally use --tool <id> and --json


openspec workset list
Show saved worksets and their members.
--json


openspec workset open <name>
Open a saved workset in its preferred tool.
--json


openspec workset remove <name>

--json



When the working root should come from a registered store rather than the current project, you can add --store <id> to commands that support it. If shared context is missing or unexpectedly empty, it may help to run openspec store doctor first. That checks the registration boundary before you inspect individual artifacts.
