title: Appendix C — GitHub Copilot Commands and OpenSpec Skills
text:
C.1 Using the matrix
OpenSpec names each workflow by its Agent Skill, while the command a developer types depends on the agent harness running it. This appendix covers GitHub Copilot inside VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA, and GitHub Copilot CLI. VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA use GitHub Copilot’s prompt-file integration. Because GitHub Copilot CLI does not read .github/prompts/, the installed skills are the appropriate option there.1
The appropriate integration can install the relevant files when you initialize the repository, for example with openspec init --tools github-copilot.2 The table uses the current OPSX command form for the Copilot extensions and the Agent Skill form for Copilot CLI. OpenSpec documents the command pattern using the apply workflow; the other workflows appear to follow the same host-specific naming pattern.3
The VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA entries match because both use the GitHub Copilot IDE integration. OpenSpec generates prompt files under .github/prompts/, which the Copilot extension can expose as slash commands in both editors.4
GitHub Copilot CLI uses the skill spelling. For example, the CLI equivalent of /opsx-apply pets-search would be /openspec-apply-change pets-search. The IDE command is not expected to resolve in the CLI because the CLI does not read .github/prompts/.5
You might use the rows as a working loop rather than as mandatory ceremony for every small edit. Explore can help when the problem or existing behavior is unclear. Propose fits once the intended change is understood well enough to record. Apply is available when the proposal is ready to execute. Sync can update the main specification while the change remains open. Archive generally follows verification and completion, when the change is ready to leave the active-work area and its deltas can become part of the lasting specs.6
The terminal CLI is a separate interface. Commands such as openspec init and openspec validate can manage the project and its artifacts from a shell. Slash commands and skills ask an AI coding tool to carry out a workflow using those artifacts. If a workflow is unavailable, it may help to check that the repository is initialized and valid and that the selected host can see the files it expects.

title: Appendix D — OpenSpec schema.yaml and Template Reference
text:
D.1 Schema fields
OpenSpec uses Schemas to configure how an OpenSpec workflow executes. This appendix can help when you need to read or change an OpenSpec workflow. It covers the fields in schema.yaml, the dependency rules between artifacts, and the way templates become generated change files.
An OpenSpec schema defines a planning workflow in YAML. It names the workflow, lists the artifacts it produces, and describes the handoff from planning to implementation. In the built-in spec-driven schema, the default sequence is explicit: proposal leads to specs and design, and tasks depends on both before implementation can begin.
The top-level fields are:
Each entry in artifacts defines one document or one set of documents:
It is useful to treat requires as a dependency graph rather than a suggested reading order. OpenSpec marks an artifact ready only after every dependency is complete. It rejects missing IDs, duplicate IDs, and dependency cycles. When several artifacts are ready at once, their order in artifacts determines which one OpenSpec returns first.
The generates value is relative to the active change directory. proposal.md therefore produces openspec/changes/<change-name>/proposal.md, while specs/**/*.md matches Markdown files below that change’s specs/ directory. Completion is structural: OpenSpec checks that the expected file exists, or that a glob matches at least one file. The check does not evaluate the document’s content.
The optional apply block controls the planning-to-implementation handoff. Its requires field names the artifacts that must exist before apply is ready. Its tracks field points to a relative Markdown file in the change directory, normally tasks.md. OpenSpec uses task checkboxes in that file to report whether work is blocked, ready, or complete. An optional instruction replaces the built-in guidance sent to the implementation agent.
The default workflow has this essential shape:
The example omits the longer agent instructions. The fields serve different purposes: description labels the artifact, template supplies its output shape, and instruction explains what the agent should produce. A changed dependency changes the workflow; a changed template changes the starting structure of every new artifact created from it.

title: Appendix D — OpenSpec schema.yaml and Template Reference
text:
D.2 Template structure
A schema directory contains schema.yaml and a templates/ directory. OpenSpec resolves the template value in each artifact entry relative to that directory:
openspec/schemas/spec-driven/
├── schema.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── proposal.md
    ├── spec.md
    ├── design.md
    └── tasks.md
Templates are Markdown skeletons rather than files copied into the change directory. OpenSpec gives the selected template to the agent as its expected output format. The agent fills that structure and writes the result at the path named by generates.
In the default schema, the mapping is:









Artifact
Template
Generated path
Purpose




proposal
proposal.md
proposal.md
Explains why the change is needed, what it changes, its capabilities, and its impact.


specs
spec.md
specs/<capability-path>/spec.md
Defines observable behavior through requirements and scenarios.


design
design.md
design.md
Explains how the change will be implemented, including decisions, risks, and trade-offs.


tasks
tasks.md
tasks.md
Breaks the implementation into ordered, checkable work items.



The specs entry is the exception to the one-file pattern. It allows a change to produce one delta specification for each capability named by the proposal. The proposal establishes the reason and scope, the spec files define behavior, the design records the technical approach, and the task list turns the plan into work the apply phase can track. Keeping these roles separate helps prevent implementation details from replacing requirements.
When a team needs different documents or a different sequence, it can create a project schema under openspec/schemas/<name>/, edit schema.yaml and the matching templates, and run openspec schema validate <name> before using it. Forking the built-in spec-driven schema copies its schema definition, templates, and instructions into a project-owned directory. A custom template changes the structure of future artifacts; a schema dependency changes which artifacts can be drafted and when. Built-in schemas ship with OpenSpec, so forking one before editing it is preferable to modifying the package copy.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.1 A diagnostic method
For each problem, start with the symptom and a likely cause. Then run the cheapest check that could distinguish between possible causes before choosing a repair. Keep the command output from that check; it may be more useful than repeating a setup step that could change the evidence.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.2 Installation failures
You might see one of these symptoms:

openspec cannot be found after npm installation.
The terminal resolves a different global npm location than expected.
Windows execution policy or macOS permissions prevent the command from running.
The installed version differs from the book’s 1.13.1 baseline.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.3 Initialization and update failures
Check whether:

OpenSpec initialized a different directory than expected.
Existing generated files conflict with the update.
The selected GitHub Copilot integration or profile is unavailable.
Project-owned configuration changed unexpectedly.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.4 Command discovery failures
You may be dealing with command discovery when:

VS Code does not show the expected prompt command.
IntelliJ IDEA does not discover the same workflow.
A prompt-file command is being confused with an Agent Skill or terminal CLI command.
The IDE appears to be using an earlier version of the generated integration files.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.5 Artifact and validation failures
The failure may be in artifact or validation handling when:

A change cannot identify its schema.
Artifact dependencies remain blocked.
Requirements or scenarios fail strict validation.
A modified requirement does not match the accepted source requirement.
Archive or sync encounters overlapping deltas.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.6 Two-repository failures
Compare the repositories when:

Frontend and backend changes use different business terms.
The generated Angular client appears stale.
The OpenAPI document does not match the backend behavior.
A test passes against a different backend or port than the one you intended.

title: Appendix E — Troubleshooting OpenSpec
text:
E.7 Recovery boundaries
Before regeneration, preserve project-owned specs and active changes. Use version control to inspect generated-file changes. If an OpenSpec defect remains reproducible, report the version, operating system, minimal repository state, command, and complete output.

title: Appendix F — Further Reading and Community Resources
text:
F.1 Official documentation
OpenSpec is open-source software available through its GitHub project and repository. Those resources include an issue queue and discussions, which can provide information about OpenSpec and Spec-Driven Development more generally.
The OpenSpec repository and its documentation are useful starting points. The OPSX workflow describes the workflow used throughout this book. The installation guide covers setup, while supported tools and aliases lists the available integrations.
These sources cover the mechanics of using OpenSpec. Your repository’s proposal, requirements, design, tasks, and verification evidence still provide the context for a specific change. The documentation can explain how a command works, but it cannot decide whether the change is understood well enough to implement or whether the resulting behavior is correct. Your project team remains responsible for the specs, and OpenSpec is more useful when the team understands them fully.

title: Appendix F — Further Reading and Community Resources
text:
F.2 Community schemas and extensions
Community-built schemas and extensions may help when the official OpenSpec workflow does not cover a particular business domain or team practice. They can also provide a working example. It is useful to treat each community-built schema as a proposal to evaluate: read its source and examples, check its maintenance activity and compatibility with your OpenSpec version, and identify the assumptions it makes about your repository and development process.
A small, representative change can provide a useful trial before the schema becomes a team convention. It helps to ask whether its artifacts make requirements easier to review, give Copilot useful context, and produce evidence that the implementation matches the intended behavior. If it adds more SDD ceremony without improving those checks, you might cherry-pick the useful ideas from the community-built schema and leave the rest behind. Recording adopted conventions in the repository gives the next developer a way to understand them.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.1 Explore unit-number search
Use these prompts as starting points. Replace bracketed decisions with the class’s agreed behavior rather than asking the agent to invent them.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text: /opsx:explore We are considering an initial commercial truck search capability. Could users search by a 15-character unit number? Please ask about exact versus partial matching, case handling, invalid input, no-match behavior, and the response shown in the UI. Hold off on creating change artifacts until those decisions are clear.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.2 Propose unit-number search

/opsx:propose add-unit-number-search Based on the exploration decisions, could you draft the proposal? Please keep implementation choices out of the behavioral requirements and include scenarios for valid input, invalid input, a match, and no match.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.3 Add VIN search

/opsx:propose add-vin-search-option Could we add a secondary search mode for a 17-character VIN while preserving unit-number search? Please ask how users would select the mode and how the two modes should share response behavior. Represent the new capability as an additive delta.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.4 Modify unit-number validation

/opsx:propose update-unit-number-length We are considering replacing the current unit-number length rule with a maximum of 10 characters. Could you identify every scenario that would change and every existing behavior that should remain intact? Represent the replacement as a modified requirement.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
section: H.5 Update an active filter proposal
text:
H.5 Update an active filter proposal

/opsx:update Could you revise the active origin-state filter change to include Active Status with values Active and Decommissioned? Please update the proposal, requirements and scenarios, design, and tasks, and flag any unanswered question about how the filters should combine.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.6 Review generated artifacts

Could you review this OpenSpec change without editing it? Please report contradictions, unsupported assumptions, missing edge cases, tasks that do not trace to requirements, and requirements that lack verification tasks.

title: Appendix H — Prompt Workbook
text:
H.7 Verify before archive

Could you compare the implemented change with the active delta and task list before archiving? Please identify unmet scenarios, code outside the approved scope, stale tasks, and tests that do not prove the specified behavior. Hold off on archiving the change.

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text: I.1 Proposal

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
Does it make the business problem and intended outcome clear?
Is the scope narrow enough to review and implement with confidence?
Does it call out the exclusions that matter for this change?
Does it leave out technical assumptions that have not been approved?
Could a reviewer tell whether this adds behavior or modifies what is already accepted?

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
I.2 Requirements and scenarios

Does each requirement describe behavior that someone could observe?
Are terms such as “maximum,” “exact,” and “optional” clear enough to avoid ambiguity?
Do the scenarios cover successful, invalid, and empty outcomes where those cases matter?
Would an additive delta leave existing behavior unchanged?
Does a modified delta include the full replacement requirement?
Could each scenario become an automated or repeatable test?

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
I.3 Design

Does it focus on decisions that have implementation consequences?
Does it explain the API, UI, validation, and persistence boundaries that may be affected?
Does it identify compatibility or migration concerns that reviewers may need to consider?
Does it record tradeoffs instead of presenting one choice as inevitable?
Does it keep from duplicating behavioral requirements?

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
I.4 Tasks

Would each task produce a visible code, test, or documentation result?
Could each requirement be traced to implementation and verification work?
Are the tasks ordered in a way that reflects their dependencies?
Are the review and test steps clear enough to follow?
Would a new agent session be able to tell what remains incomplete?

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
I.5 Apply review

Does the implementation appear to match the latest artifacts rather than an earlier chat message?
Are the frontend and backend validation rules consistent with one another?
Do the tests demonstrate the scenarios rather than only executing lines?
Has the agent changed code outside the approved scope?
Does the task list reflect what has actually been completed?

title: Appendix I — Artifact Review Checklists
text:
I.6 Archive readiness

Has the team accepted the final behavior?
Do the affected tests pass?
Would the main spec remain coherent after the delta merges?
Have overlapping active changes been reviewed against the new baseline?
Is any unfinished work represented by a separate tracked change?

J.2 Teaching checkpoints
It may help to measure progress by more than whether the agent generated files. Pause at these points:

After exploration, ask which ambiguities a person resolved.
After proposal, invite participants to separate behavior from implementation.
After apply, consider tracing one scenario through UI, API, persistence, and test code.

title: Appendix J — Instructor Guide
text:
J.3 Expected friction
Participants may type slash commands into the terminal, accept generated assumptions, or treat task checkmarks as test results. Keeping the terminal/chat distinction visible can help, as can asking for an artifact review before each apply or archive step.
Tool output may differ across OpenSpec releases or coding-agent models. Teach the invariant workflow and review criteria rather than requiring identical generated prose.

title: Appendix J — Instructor Guide
text:
J.4 Recovery points
Maintain three instructor baselines:

Baseline A: Initialized project with no truck-search spec.
Baseline B: Archived unit-number search.
Baseline C: Archived VIN search and 10-character unit-number rule.

These baselines can keep a setup problem from consuming the next morning. They also let the instructor demonstrate a delta against a known source of truth.

title: Appendix J — Instructor Guide
text:
J.5 Closing discussion
Ask participants to name one change in their own codebase where conflicting interpretations would cost more than writing a short spec. Then ask for one change too small or reversible to justify the workflow. The contrast can help keep SDD grounded as an engineering tradeoff rather than a universal ceremony.
